items.title: Centene lifts annual profit forecast, reports upbeat third-quarter results
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Health insurer Centene raised its annual profit forecast on Tuesday and reported better-than-expected third-quarter results.
items.body:
Health insurer Centene (CNC.N) raised its annual profit forecast on Tuesday and reported better-than-expected third-quarter results.
Health insurers have grappled with rising medical costs in recent years as patients seek more care, putting pressure on profits and prompting companies to focus on cost controls.
Centene's medical loss ratio, the percentage of premiums spent on medical care, came in at 92.7% in the third quarter, unchanged from last year. Analysts has expected the company to report a ratio of 92.84%.
"Solid underlying fundamentals within our core businesses have powered a faster recovery to our earnings trajectory than previously anticipated," said Centene CEO Sarah M. London.
The company now sees 2026 adjusted profit to be more than $5.20 per share, higher than its previous expectation of more than $4.80 per share. Analysts expected a profit of $4.88, per data compiled by LSEG.
items.raw_description: Health insurer Centene raised its annual profit forecast on Tuesday and reported better-than-expected third-quarter results.

items.title: Hilton raises annual room revenue growth forecast on steady US travel demand
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Hotel operator Hilton Worldwide Holdings raised annual room revenue growth forecast on Tuesday, betting that steady US travel demand will support growth across its properties.
items.body:
Hotel operator Hilton Worldwide Holdings (HLT.N) raised annual room revenue growth forecast on Tuesday, betting that steady US travel demand will support growth across its properties.
Wealthy consumers continued to spend on luxury experiences, while demand for mid-scale and budget hotels also improved during the quarter as leisure travel held up despite stubborn inflation and geopolitical uncertainty, including the conflict in the Middle East.
Business travel also remained robust, benefiting hotel operators such as Hilton.
Spending on travel, according to US Travel Association, rose 2.5% in August compared with the year-ago period.
Hilton's revenue per available room, or revPAR, at its luxury properties Waldorf Astoria and LXR rose 13.9% and 14.3% respectively, during the quarter.
The McLean, Virginia-based company expects revenue per available room — a key lodging metric that tracks average daily rate and occupancy — to grow between 4% and 4.5% for fiscal 2026, compared with its previous forecast of a 3% to 3.5% increase.
items.raw_description: Hotel operator Hilton Worldwide Holdings raised annual room revenue growth forecast on Tuesday, betting that steady US travel demand will support growth across its properties.

items.title: Britain's FTSE 100 falls as HSBC drags banks lower
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Britain's FTSE 100 slumped on Tuesday, pressured by HSBC shares after its quarterly revenue miss, while investors remained cautious ahead of the government's budget and amid higher oil prices.
items.body:
Britain's FTSE 100 slumped on Tuesday, pressured by HSBC shares after its quarterly revenue miss, while investors remained cautious ahead of the government's budget and amid higher oil prices.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index (.FTSE) fell 0.76% to 10,685.18 points by 0949 GMT, heading towards its biggest one-day decline in about a month. The midcap FTSE 250 (.FTMC) gained 0.16%.
HSBC (HSBA.L) fell 7%, its steepest one-day percentage decline since April 2025. Europe's largest bank reported third-quarter revenue of $18.6 billion, missing analysts' estimates of $19 billion, hurt by a [USN:L2N46D02S TEXT:"slowdown"] in its wealth business
Standard Chartered (STAN.L) , NatWest Group (NWG.L) and Lloyds Banking Group (LLOY.L) fell between 1.1% and 2.2%
The banking index (.FTNMX301010) hit a four-month low and was last down 3.7%
Brent crude gained 0.4% on renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, overshadowing optimism from talks in Tehran
[USN:L8N4690JW TEXT:"Britain's budget"] is due on Wednesday, with investors remaining cautious ahead of key fiscal announcements against the backdrop of high borrowing costs and energy prices
British business minister Jonathan Reynolds said Britain and the EU were "finding a way through" concerns over the bloc's proposed "Made in Europe" rules, which have raised [USN:L5N46D0G5 TEXT:"uncertainty for UK manufacturers"]
Exhibitions group Informa (INF.L) slipped 1% after cutting its full-year revenue growth guidance to 3% from 6%, as security concerns in the Middle East forced the [USN:L6N46D0EH TEXT:"rescheduling "]of events in Saudi Arabia
Dettol maker Reckitt (RKT.L) fell 4.5% after [USN:L6N46D0E0 TEXT:"cutting"] its annual net revenue growth forecast, dragging the personal care, drug and grocery sector (.FTNMX452010) 1.8% lower into negative territory
Computacenter (CCC.L) was the top gainer on the FTSE 100, rising 1.6% after Stifel [USN:FWN46D0ER TEXT:"raised"] its price target on the IT services provider

items.title: Irak Six Français condamnés à la perpétuité pour appartenance à l'EI
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Un tribunal irakien a condamné mardi six ressortissants français à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité et un septième à 15 ans de prison pour appartenance au groupe Etat islamique.
items.body:
Un tribunal irakien a condamné mardi six ressortissants français à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité et un septième à 15 ans de prison pour appartenance au groupe Etat islamique.
Ces sept hommes sont au nombre des 47 membres présumés de l'EI d'origine française transférés des geôles du nord-est de la Syrie en Irak en 2025 dans le cadre d'un accord sécuritaire supervisé par l'armée américaine.
Au terme de ce procès ouvert en septembre dernier, les combattants islamistes ont été condamnés en vertu de la loi anti-terroriste irakienne. Le président du tribunal a précisé que la perpétuité avait été préférée à la peine capitale dans leur cas en raison de leur jeune âge, a rapporté un journaliste de Reuters présent à l'audience.
On ignore l'âge des six condamnés à la réclusion à perpétuité, mais le septième accusé est âgé de 23 ans.
L'un de leurs avocats, Me Abbas al-Maliki, a précisé qu'un appel serait formé auprès de la Cour de cassation irakienne.
items.raw_description: Un tribunal irakien a condamné mardi six ressortissants français à la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité et un septième à 15 ans de prison pour appartenance au groupe Etat islamique.

items.title: UPS raises annual profit, revenue forecasts as higher-paying shipments boost margin
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: United Parcel Service raised its full-year profit and revenue forecast on Tuesday, as higher-margin international air shipments aided profits following its decision to cut millions of lower-margin deliveries for its largest customer, Amazon.com .
items.body:
United Parcel Service (UPS.N) raised its full-year profit and revenue forecast on Tuesday, as higher-margin international air shipments aided profits following its decision to cut millions of lower-margin deliveries for its largest customer, Amazon.com (AMZN.O) .
Atlanta-based UPS now expects 2026 adjusted profit of around $7.28 per share, compared with $7.22 it had forecast in July.
The company expects annual revenue of $92.6 billion, compared with its previous projection of $91.2 billion.

items.summary: Maruti Suzuki reported a smaller-than-expected quarterly profit on Tuesday as cost pressures linked to rising prices of raw materials squeezed margins.
items.body:
Maruti Suzuki (MRTI.NS) reported a smaller-than-expected quarterly profit on Tuesday as cost pressures linked to rising prices of raw materials squeezed margins.
India's top carmaker by sales reported a profit of 24.15 billion rupees ($253.85 million) for the July to September quarter, below analysts' average estimates of 31.05 billion rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG.

items.title: Bayern's Kompany is improving but no comeback date yet, says assistant coach Danks
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany is improving following a collapse in training last week and there is no date for his return yet, assistant coach Aaron Danks said on Tuesday.
items.body:
Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany is improving following a collapse in training last week and there is no date for his return yet, assistant coach Aaron Danks said on Tuesday.
The Belgian was [USN:L6N469124 TEXT:"rushed to hospital"] on Friday after collapsing during a reserve-team training session and is expected to be [USN:L6N46A02I TEXT:"sidelined for weeks"]. The 40-year-old had been battling a virus in recent days and had missed some training sessions before his collapse.
"I paid him a short visit yesterday," Danks told a press conference ahead of Wednesday's German Cup second round against visitors Magdeburg.
"He is in good spirits. It looks like every day he is getting better. There are no major updates in terms of diagnosis or return to work. Let him rest, let him take his time."
The German champions have a busy match schedule with Magdeburg on Wednesday, followed by the Klassiker against title rivals Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga on Saturday. They then travel to Madrid in the Champions League next week to face Atletico.
"We had some good conversations (with Kompany) but kept it away from football and specific tactics," Danks said. "It was just a friendly chat and nice to see him and catch up."
The assistant coach said Kompany's health scare coupled with Monday's [USN:L2N46C15E TEXT:"Ballon d'Or win"] for Bayern striker Harry Kane reflected a rollercoaster of emotions for a squad that has shown the necessary team spirit to stay on course.
Kane is the first Englishman to win the prestigious award in 25 years, after Michael Owen won it in 2001.
"For us, we are super professional," Danks said. "Full extremes of life in the last week. Joys and highs for Harry and the lows of the last days."
"To get through these moments we had to rely on our chemistry, our team spirit and that definitely helped us," he added.

items.title: Fashion's AI era: face swaps and digital clones
items.author: Helen Reid
items.creator: Helen Reid
items.summary: AI-generated fashion models present a tantalizing opportunity for brands: the ability to create lifelike images for their retail websites while cutting costs by 90% or more compared to photo shoots with human models.
items.body:
AI-generated fashion models present a tantalizing opportunity for brands: the ability to create lifelike images for their retail websites while cutting costs by 90% or more compared to photo shoots with human models.
For the modeling industry, the technology poses an existential threat because of scant regulation governing the ownership or use of digital twins. Fashion models face the risk of unpaid replication of their image – or replacement by entirely synthetic models.
To understand how AI is upending the economics of fashion modeling, Reuters interviewed 15 model-agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential photo-shoot contracts in which brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal (OREP.PA) detailed proposed terms for AI-created alterations and future use of the images.
The companies’ contract requests included the right to swap a model's face with another using AI; the creation of a digital clone with no additional compensation to the model; and the right to use images of a model's body to train AI. The terms in the unsigned contracts also included broad legal language that could effectively give a brand leeway to use AI however it wanted.
While some companies are looking to repurpose or modify images of existing models, others are using fully AI-generated models, not based on existing humans.
As AI use expands, modeling agencies are seeing bookings decline, photo studios are closing and models are facing the loss of a chunk of their livelihoods: photo shoots by fast-fashion retailers constantly adding new collections to their websites.
"Within a year, even the next six months, there's going to be less jobs for models, especially our bread and butter, which is ecommerce," said Adot Gak, a model based in London who has been on the cover of Harper's Bazaar and appeared in campaigns by brands including Balmain and H&M. "If we don't speak up about this, in the next two years the whole industry will just be bots."
While some fast-fashion players like Spain’s Mango have already rolled out AI-generated models at scale, high-end brands are moving more cautiously. Moncler experimented early with an AI-generated campaign in 2023, and Gucci caused controversy in fashion circles when it posted images generated by AI on Instagram this year.
Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models, either on its website or in its campaigns. Gucci did not respond to requests for comment.
"The scariest part is that now people cannot differentiate between a real model and an AI model," said Gak.
FACE SWAPS AND 'DIGITAL TWINS' AI allows retailers to endlessly rework and redeploy a model’s image wearing different outfits at a fraction of the cost of new shoots.
"Some brands ask to modify faces, bodies, skin, age or expressions after shoots using AI. Others are asking about creating 'digital twins' of models that they can reuse later without needing another production," said Patrick Staal, owner of modeling agency Uniko Models in Barcelona.
In a photo-shoot casting sheet, Italian brand Diesel asked models to agree to "alteration or reconstruction of facial features and body proportions,” along with “swapping of faces among the participating models,” and “superimposition of the Participant’s face onto another person’s body.”
Diesel's parent company OTB told Reuters the model release was drafted for a specific campaign and isn’t representative of its typical agreements. It said it doesn’t systematically modify models with AI.
Reale Actives – the skincare brand launched this year by social-media personality Alix Earle – uses the tagline, "Reale you is perfect you."
But in a contract seen by Reuters, the brand asked for rights to create AI-generated replicas of models and to "own" and use these fakes for a year without further compensation.
Reale Actives said in a statement that it uses real models and hasn’t replicated any model using AI. It said the contract language came from a partner production company, which it declined to name.
MODELS TRAINING THEIR MACHINE REPLACEMENTS? In some cases, models are helping to train their replacements: some contracts’ fine print includes language allowing the use of their images to train AI tools.
A Calvin Klein draft contract seen by Reuters asked the model to accept, for no extra pay, that the brand “may use reasonably unrecognizable images of Model (no identifying features such as Model's face, scars, tattoos or otherwise) to train and fine tune AI tools for learning general model attributes.”
A Calvin Klein spokesperson said in a statement: "Like many others, we are testing and learning in this fast-moving space," adding that the brand's AI use is guided by regulation, industry standards and respect for models' rights.
In many cases, contracts include wording such as "including" or "not limited to," which lawyers commonly use to claim rights that aren’t spelled out.
Melanie Howard, partner and chair of luxury brands at law firm Loeb & Loeb in Los Angeles, represents both brands and talent in contract negotiations and said such sweeping language "is dangerous in its ambiguity” and makes it difficult for models to challenge any unsanctioned use of their images.
In a photo-shoot contract seen by Reuters, France’s L'Oreal asked for "the right to use artificial intelligence (AI) technologies... including for the purpose of modifying, enhancing, or adapting the appearance of cosmetic products, packaging, or shades, as well as for retouching purposes."
Without addressing that contract language, L'Oreal said it uses standard AI tools in post-production and editing that don't affect the model's image.
'WE ARE SAVING SO MUCH MONEY' Some firms are openly embracing AI to replace models and save money.
Europe's biggest online-fashion retailer, Zalando, has rapidly [USN:L8N3RE3M7 TEXT:"adopted AI-generated imagery"] for marketing content – and shut both its photo studios in Berlin last year. Fast-fashion retailer About You, which Zalando acquired in July last year, also closed its studio. Overall, Zalando cut more than 340 jobs, though the company said it retained some of those employees in other roles.
Now, About You is launching its Scayle Studios business, which creates digital imagery for other retailers using AI-generated models and promises a more than 90% production-cost reduction. Scayle has 130 brand clients and has generated 190,000 outfits in the last month, according to a company spokesperson.
"We are saving so much money," said Julian Jansen, vice president of marketing at About You. "You've always had this super fast world of ecommerce, and this super slow traditional world of photo shoots, it didn't fit together in any way – and now with AI, it's a completely different scale."
LITTLE REGULATION Regulations globally haven’t kept pace with the threat to models’ livelihoods, but the New York State Fashion Workers Act is one exception. The law has made it illegal since June 2025 for brands to create or modify replicas of models without their explicit consent.
"The misuse of models' images is not new, but with AI that problem is accelerated tenfold," said Sara Ziff, founder and executive director of the New York-based nonprofit Model Alliance, which backed the legislation.
Ziff, herself a model for years, pushes for similar laws in other states and federally.
The British Fashion Model Agents Association has drawn up an AI code of practice, including that AI can only be used with the consent of a model, who would own any digital twin. But BFMA head John Horner said that without binding regulation in Britain or Europe, models still risk being taken advantage of by less scrupulous agents.
"A lot of young talents don’t fully understand the long-term consequences yet," said Staal, the Barcelona-based model agency director. "Signing away AI rights at 20 years old could still affect someone ten years later."

items.title: The ultra-wealthy crypto executives who are spending big on the midterms
items.author: Hannah Lang
items.creator: Hannah Lang
items.summary: A clutch of ultra-wealthy executives who made fortunes in and around the cryptocurrency business have become influential players in US politics, collectively spending more than $56 million during the current election cycle so far, according to a Reuters analysis of federal filings.
items.body:
A clutch of ultra-wealthy executives who made fortunes in and around the cryptocurrency business have become influential players in US politics, collectively spending more than $56 million during the current election cycle so far, according to a Reuters analysis of federal filings.
They have spent on crypto-friendly candidates and crypto super political action committees, or PACs, that [USN:L1N4310KM TEXT:"can raise and spend unlimited sums"], contributing towards the industry's [USN:L6N45Z0W4 TEXT:"$175 million blitz"] this cycle, according to federal filings.
However, a large chunk of the spending extends beyond digital assets to candidates and fundraising vehicles aligned with their views on issues ranging from technology, innovation and energy policy, to taxation and economic growth.
Below are the crypto executives who have spent at least $500,000 on the 2025-2026 cycle, according to the most recently available Federal Election Commission filings.
Totals include contributions to candidates, party committees and PACs, and certain donations made through affiliated entities. They do not include donations to "dark money" political nonprofits, which are not required to disclose donors.
Reuters excluded routine transfers from joint fundraising committees to avoid double-counting.
All the individuals named below either declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment.
CAMERON AND TYLER WINKLEVOSS, CO-FOUNDERS OF GEMINI SPACE STATION (GEMI.O)
Crypto entrepreneurs Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss have contributed nearly $13 million each this cycle, mostly to MAGA Inc, the main super PAC supporting President Donald Trump.
The twins are also the primary backers of the Digital Freedom Fund (DFF), a super PAC that has been [USN:L1N45O0KN TEXT:"spending this cycle to oppose Democratic candidate"] and crypto skeptic Sherrod Brown, who is running for a US Senate seat in Ohio.
Winklevoss Capital Fund, the twins' venture capital and family office, contributed $21.3 million to DFF this cycle.
BRIAN ARMSTRONG, CEO AND CO-FOUNDER OF COINBASE (COIN.O)
Armstrong, one of the crypto industry's most high-profile advocates, has contributed roughly $1 million to federal candidates, party committees and PACs, dishing the cash out roughly evenly to both parties. He also made five-figure donations to an array of congressional candidates on both sides of the aisle.
CHRIS LARSEN, CO-FOUNDER AND EXECUTIVE CHAIRMAN OF RIPPLE LABS Larsen, a co-founder of blockchain payments firm Ripple Labs, has spent at least $14.6 million this cycle, mostly on Democratic-aligned and issue-focused groups. That included a $6 million donation to the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC, which backs candidates supportive of renewable energy. He also donated $4.5 million to You Can Push Back PAC, which focuses on artificial intelligence safety.
MARC ANDREESSEN AND BEN HOROWITZ, CO-FOUNDERS AND GENERAL PARTNERS OF ANDREESSEN HOROWITZ Andreessen and Horowitz's eponymous venture capital firm has made major investments in crypto companies, including Coinbase, as well as AI companies.
Andreessen gave $3 million to MAGA Inc and roughly $719,000 in other contributions to mostly Republican-leaning party committees, leadership PACs and candidates.
Horowitz also contributed $3 million to MAGA Inc and nearly $1 million to party committees and candidates, including almost $215,000 to the National Republican Senatorial Committee.
MIKE NOVOGRATZ, CEO AND FOUNDER OF GALAXY DIGITAL (GLXY.O)
An early bitcoin investor and champion of the cryptocurrency, Novogratz has donated at least $1.9 million this cycle, mostly to Democratic-leaning and independent expenditure groups. That includes about $780,000 to Next Generation Action PAC, which focuses on electing younger Democratic candidates, and $250,000 to The Bench PAC, another Democratic-aligned group.
CHRIS DIXON, GENERAL PARTNER AT ANDREESSEN HOROWITZ Dixon, the founder of Andreessen Horowitz's dedicated crypto and blockchain venture arm a16z crypto, has donated roughly $867,000 across Republican and Democratic campaign committees, candidates, leadership PACs and crypto-related groups.
MATT HUANG, CO-FOUNDER AND MANAGING PARTNER AT PARADIGM Huang, co-founder of crypto and AI-focused investment firm Paradigm, has contributed at least $831,000, largely to Republican candidates and committees.
CHARLES CASCARILLA, CEO AND CO-FOUNDER OF PAXOS Cascarilla, CEO of stablecoin and blockchain infrastructure firm Paxos, has contributed roughly $642,000, with the majority supporting Republican candidates via the party's main committees and other PACs.
items.raw_description: A clutch of ultra-wealthy executives who made fortunes in and around the cryptocurrency business have become influential players in US politics, collectively spending more than $56 million during the current election cycle so far, according to a Reuters analysis of federal filings.

items.title: Mapping the Market: Oil may be in for a slide
items.author: Robert Fullem
items.creator: Robert Fullem
items.summary: US crude oil prices are holding near the top of this year's range. Trading during the Iran war suggests lasting gains from here will be hard to come by, and technical analysis points to possible losses.
items.body:
US crude oil prices are holding near the top of this year's range. Trading during the Iran war suggests lasting gains from here will be hard to come by, and technical analysis points to possible losses.
Click here for a detailed technical analysis chart.
Technical analysis uses charts of past price moves to work out where a market might go next. Over the years, analysts have identified recurring chart patterns that tend to come before gains or losses.
One of those patterns is called a gap. Gaps form when prices jump or drop so fast that they skip over a range of price levels, leaving an empty space on the chart.
They often show up between one day's closing price and the next day's opening price. Many analysts believe markets tend to return eventually to fill a gap, meaning they trade back through the skipped range.
Volatile trading during the Iran war left several gaps on the chart of the US oil price, which is traded as West Texas Intermediate.
Most have since been filled, but at least two remain partly or completely open. Both sit below current prices, which suggests the market's path of least resistance may be down. That raises expectations that they will eventually be filled.
Analysts also look for levels that act as support and resistance. Support works like a floor that can stop prices from falling. Resistance works like a ceiling that can cap gains.
Both can become price targets, meaning levels where traders expect the market to head or pause. Gaps can serve as support, resistance and targets too.
The gap closest to the market — which has been trading around $100 — lies between the August 28 close of $83.40, according to data supplied by LSEG, and the August 31 open of $84.69. That is roughly $15 below current prices.
A drop to that area would put the market back inside the empty space left by the August jump.
The second gap is larger, but it has also been partially filled. It lies between the February 27 close of $67.02 and the March 2 open of $75.00. This was the market's opening reaction to the war, when prices leapt over an $8 range in a single step.
A fall that far would take oil back to levels last seen before the conflict began.
One cautionary note: Gaps are not guarantees. Markets can leave gaps open for long periods, and a prolonged conflict or supply disruption could keep crude prices elevated.
But with oil stalling near the top of its yearly range, the unfilled gaps below give sellers a clear set of targets.
What the chart shows:
US crude is trading near the top of this year's range, around $100
Two unfilled gaps lie below the market: $83.40-$84.69 and $67.02-$75.00
Markets often return to fill gaps, so those zones could act as downside targets
(Mapping the Market is a daily column written by Reuters journalists. The commentary is based on a technical analysis of financial charts, which helps assess the likelihood of future price moves but does not guarantee the outcome. The column does not constitute investment advice or trading recommendations. )

items.title: Last Republican incumbent senator in a Democratic-leaning state fights for survival
items.author: Andy Sullivan
items.creator: Andy Sullivan
items.summary: If Republican Senator Susan Collins wins this nail-biter of an election, it may well be because voters in Maine decide she is not Republican enough.
items.body:
If Republican Senator Susan Collins wins this nail-biter of an election, it may well be because voters in Maine decide she is not Republican enough.
Since her first victory in 1996, Collins’ reputation as an independent-minded moderate has helped her win reelection even as Maine backed Democrats for president. Now the only Republican incumbent running in a Democratic-leaning state, she is deadlocked in opinion polls with Democrat Troy Jackson in a race that could help determine control of the US Senate.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the 100-seat Senate from Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections . Jackson, a rough-hewn former logger and state Senate president, has attacked Collins as a rubber stamp for Republican President Donald Trump .
Collins is countering with the clout she has amassed over her 30-year Senate career, highlighting projects she has funded and carve-outs she has secured to lessen the [USN:L1N4680R7 TEXT:"economic fallout"] from Trump’s spending cuts, tariffs and war with Iran.
“If it wasn't Susan Collins, this race would have been over three months ago,” said Maine Democratic consultant Toby McGrath.
But strategists in both parties say the pool of the independent-minded, persuadable voters who backed Collins in previous elections has shrunk as partisan lines have hardened and Trump has galvanized Democrats in opposition.
“If you hate Trump, you're voting for whoever the Democrats put on the ballot,” said Phil Harriman, a former Republican state senator.
Democrats faced a potential debacle this summer, when Graham Platner, an oyster farmer and Marine veteran, won the party’s nomination [USN:S0N42B09J TEXT:"only to drop out"] after facing a rape accusation that he denied.
The party quickly united behind Jackson, who has invoked his hardscrabble upbringing in the remote logging town of Allagash as he campaigns on a populist agenda of universal healthcare and raising taxes on the wealthy.
“I saw at a young age how people with money and power and influence can hold people back,” he said at a campaign event on Saturday.
$1.5 BILLION IN EARMARKS In recent weeks, Collins has visited projects she has funded through her work on the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee: a wastewater treatment plant in North Windham, a dock in Bucksport, an emergency center in Farmington. She says she has secured nearly $1.5 billion in earmarks since 2021.
“This has required hard work, knowledge and seniority. The question for voters in this campaign is who can do more for Maine,” she said at an October 15 debate.
That influence, she argues, has also helped to shield Maine from the Trump administration’s policies.
As Trump’s [USN:L6N4580Y1 TEXT:"trade war with Canada"] has hammered the state’s economy, Collins has pointed to tariff exemptions the administration has granted at her request for road salt, cement and equipment used by the state’s blueberry, potato and apple growers.
The Trump administration also credited her when it released home-heating oil reserves to try to drive down prices that have increased more than 70% since last year – a [USN:L6N461155 TEXT:"crucial issue"] in a state where roughly half of households rely on the product.
Collins has also pointed to a $50 billion fund she crafted to help [USN:L6N3S70P7 TEXT:"rural hospitals"] cope with healthcare cuts in the 2025 tax and spending package that enacted most of Trump’s legislative agenda, as well as money for body-worn cameras and de-escalation training for federal immigration agents following the January killing of two US citizens in Minnesota.
'THERE SHOULDN'T BE A LIST' Jackson argues that these carve-outs amount to little when weighed against the damage caused by Trump.
Body cameras and de-escalation training did not stop an immigration agent from [USN:L6N43H0SA TEXT:"killing a state resident"] in July, he says, and residents would not be struggling to heat their homes if Trump had not started the war with Iran, which has pushed up oil prices globally.
Trump’s trade war with Canada, he argues, is only possible because Republicans in Congress have surrendered their authority over tariffs to Trump.
“I can't believe that the most powerful US senator in the world would stand there and say, 'Well, I got this and this and that off the list,' instead of the fact that there shouldn’t be a list,” he said on Saturday.
SIX ADS IN A ROW Meanwhile, a relentless ad war has played out over the state’s airwaves. AdImpact, an analysis firm, estimates $199 million will be spent on the race – equal to $170 for every adult in the state.
During a local newscast on Friday, six ads in a row were devoted to the contest.
Those ads are chasing a small slice of undecided voters.
Democratic activists say they are encountering relatively few people who have yet to decide on a candidate as they campaign door-to-door in Windham, a Portland suburb that backed Collins by a 14-point margin in 2020, even as it backed Democrat Joe Biden over Trump for president.
“There’s just a lot less of that persuadable middle than we historically see,” said volunteer Austin Coco.
Windham resident Jim Tabor, a retired optician, said he has grown disillusioned with the Republican Party under Trump. A Collins supporter in past elections, he said this year he will back Jackson.
“If he turns out to be a bum, I’ll vote against him next time. But Susan Collins won’t be there,” he said.
items.raw_description: If Republican Senator Susan Collins wins this nail-biter of an election, it may well be because voters in Maine decide she is not Republican enough.

items.title: Hold or sell? High Treasury yields spur US banks to rethink bond portfolios - Reuters

items.raw_description: Hold or sell? High Treasury yields spur US banks to rethink bond portfolios    Reuters

items.title: Hold or sell? High Treasury yields spur US banks to rethink bond portfolios
items.author: Manya Saini, Arasu Basil, Niket Nishant
items.creator: Manya Saini, Arasu Basil, Niket Nishant
items.summary: A spike in Treasury yields is forcing US banks to confront an uncomfortable question: sell bonds worth billions of dollars they own at a loss, or hold on to paper losses?
items.body:
A spike in Treasury yields is forcing US banks to confront an uncomfortable question: sell bonds worth billions of dollars they own at a loss, or hold on to paper losses?
Both carry costs. Selling involves taking an immediate financial hit, while waiting would pile on losses on the balance sheet that can weaken some measures of financial strength and limit payouts to shareholders.
"Persistent higher rates or a steepening long end would prolong the drag and keep pressure on tangible equity, and for some banks, regulatory capital," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which holds several bank stocks.
Banks record changes in the value of bonds they might sell before maturity under an accounting measure known as accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI). It reflects gains or losses that have not yet been realized through a sale.
The industry's AOCI balance remained deeply negative at $156.64 billion in the second quarter, despite improving substantially from 2023 levels, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data.
That was before the 10-year US Treasury yield, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, posted its sharpest rise since 1994 in the third quarter, potentially deepening the losses.
Bank of America's (BAC.N) accumulated other comprehensive loss swelled by over $3 billion in the three months ended September 30, compared with the end of June.
The bank had unrealized losses on its bond portfolio of [USN:L4N4600XY TEXT:"$109 billion"] at the end of September, up from $85 billion at June-end. The bulk of these securities were in the held-to-maturity segment, which the bank does not intend to sell.
SELL NOW OR WAIT? Treasury yields and bond prices move inversely. As yields rise, prices of existing bonds fall, deepening unrealized losses reflected in AOCI.
"Given the movement in rates, it may be worth it to take a loss and then redeploy that capital at higher yields, which would benefit cash flow and capital generation in the future," said Macrae Sykes, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds.
The risks associated with bond portfolios are not entirely hypothetical. Deep losses on bond investments, combined with customers rapidly withdrawing deposits, contributed to the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Although banks have since trimmed their exposure, the latest jump in yields shows how decisions made years ago can continue to be a drag.
"A bank should be willing to realize a loss if the higher yield on replacement assets earns the loss back over a reasonable horizon," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
SHARE REPURCHASES COULD STALL The impact is already showing on plans to return money to shareholders.
Fifth Third (FITB.N) said it delayed a planned share repurchase in September after a sharp rise in interest rates affected its AOCI.
Wells Fargo (WFC.N) also said future buybacks may depend partly on how rates impact its investments.
"Looking ahead, we will continue to consider the interest rate environment and the impact on accumulated other comprehensive income in determining how much stock we repurchase," Chief Financial Officer Mike Santomassimo told analysts.
Meanwhile, Truist (TFC.N) has been repositioning its securities portfolio, with Chief Financial Officer Mike Maguire saying the bank sees scope for further sales but that the pool of actionable bonds is finite.
"With Basel III really coming into focus and in sight, we do feel like it's sensible to take action around the securities portfolio."
Basel III refers to an international framework which could influence how banks manage their investments and how much money they can return to shareholders. The rules could add another layer of complexity to banks' decisions on how to manage their bond portfolios.
PNC executives also said the bank is factoring in Basel III capital rules, which are "just around the corner," as it evaluates its AOCI holdings.

items.title: Bond investors are thinking less about the Fed and more about AI, deficits
items.author: Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss
items.creator: Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss
items.summary: Wall Street considers it settled that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates steady this week. Whether that spells good news for Treasuries is more complicated.
items.body:
Wall Street considers it settled that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates steady this week. Whether that spells good news for Treasuries is more complicated.
After a bruising selloff that took yields up sharply for two months starting in August, the Treasury market has rallied, reflecting concern that financing troubles in a corner of the market [USN:l6n4690sj TEXT:"for AI infrastructure"] could slow the artificial intelligence buildout that is a central driver of the US economy. Yields [USN:l6n4681a9 TEXT:"have come down from the highs"] they hit early in October.
But analysts and portfolio managers stress that many of the forces that have [USN:l6n45n0y4 TEXT:"made bond investors miserable this year"] — stubborn inflation, heavy government and corporate borrowing, and uncertainty over next week's [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"] — remain in place. That makes it difficult to forecast what the rest of 2026 holds for a market where prices are still down significantly for the year.
"I don't think the Fed is entirely in the driver's seat in today's market. Increasingly, the bigger story is the AI-driven investment cycle and what happens to risk sentiment around it," said Christian Hoffmann, head of fixed income at Thornburg Investment Management.
"In recent trading, capital has moved out of some AI-related trades and into bonds in what looks like a flight to quality, and flows like that can overwhelm relatively small changes in Fed expectations."
FEW EXPECT A RATE INCREASE Investors expect the Fed to stay on hold but to raise rates again in December. The decision may be less important than what officials signal about inflation and the path of rates in the months ahead, investors said. Markets have repeatedly swung between expectations for policy easing and tightening on concerns that persistent price pressures could force the Fed to keep borrowing costs elevated for longer.
The benchmark 10-year yield has risen 84 basis points this year, on track for its largest yearly increase since 2022. US 30-year yields are up nearly 50 basis points in 2026, their biggest yearly rise since 2024.
Of late, comments from Fed officials John Williams and Philip Jefferson [USN:l6n46518p TEXT:"helped to reset investor expectations towards fewer near-term rate hikes"]. Both sit on the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee. But few have forgotten that consumer and producer prices rose in August and September, with higher energy prices -- which remain elevated -- as one of the main culprits.
"Inflation has clearly re-accelerated so to us this isn't necessarily a pause, but just to see how some of this data changes given the recent hike," said Jack Herr, senior investment analyst at GuideStone Funds. "The Fed will probably hike again this year."
FISCAL HEADWINDS Even if the Fed stays on hold, the long end of the curve -- bonds with maturities of 10 or more years -- could remain under pressure. JPMorgan's latest Treasury Client Survey showed client positioning with the fewest outright longs since mid-August, reflecting reduced betting on lower yields.
That outlook reflects in part the government's growing financing need, with a worsening fiscal backdrop and the $40 trillion national debt contributing to bouts of volatility.
Treasury issuance has surged alongside widening budget deficits, increasing the amount of debt that private investors must absorb. The steady increase in supply has become an important driver of longer-term yields and has at times overshadowed changes in Fed policy expectations.
"It's hard to have a lot of confidence in exactly what's going to happen from here, especially when you're looking at ongoing deficits on the order of 6% of GDP (gross domestic product)," said Chris Maxey, chief market strategist at Wealthspire Advisors.
"Our net debt interest costs could actually consume more of our deficit, and that begins to squeeze out other spending that happens. That could naturally push yields higher across the curve because there's just that fiscal concern element."
Many investors took the intensity of the late summer bond rout as a shot across the bow of policy makers, but even those who believe the message was received say it will take time to change the momentum on spending in Washington.
"Regardless of the election results, we should not probably expect any meaningful fiscal restraint," said Oli Shale, US investment specialist at asset manager Ruffer. "More spending is the path of least resistance and this regime is not going anywhere for some time."

items.title: Países Bajos no participará en el Festival de Eurovisión de 2027 en protesta contra Israel
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Países Bajos no participará en el Festival de la Canción de Eurovisión de 2027, ya que ninguna cadena está dispuesta a asumir la responsabilidad de la candidatura neerlandesa debido a la preocupación por la participación de Israel, informó el martes la asociación de cadenas NPO.
items.body:
Países Bajos no participará en el Festival de la Canción de Eurovisión de 2027, ya que ninguna cadena está dispuesta a asumir la responsabilidad de la candidatura neerlandesa debido a la preocupación por la participación de Israel, informó el martes la asociación de cadenas NPO.
El mes pasado, la NPO dijo que confiaba en que Países Bajos volvería al concurso al año que viene, tras el boicot a la edición de 2026, ya que consideraba que la Unión Europea de Radiodifusión había respondido a las críticas de los países que no habían participado en 2026.
Sin embargo, al final ninguna cadena neerlandesa se mostró dispuesta a hacer posible la candidatura neerlandesa.
Irlanda, Islandia, España, Eslovenia y Países Bajos boicotearon el concurso en mayo en protesta por la participación de Israel y su ofensiva militar en Gaza.

items.title: Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
items.author: Raphael Satter
items.creator: Raphael Satter
items.summary: Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink's satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
items.body:
Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink's satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro (4704.T) , concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX's Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.
The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI's telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people's browsers and apps.
SpaceX (SPCX.O) did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks.
TrendAI released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.
TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding "hype-driven labels" or "unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions."
Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become [USN:L5N46A00R TEXT:"a particularly important resource"] in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"for frontline communications"] and [USN:L8N4350JH TEXT:"directing drone strikes"].
In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
DISCOVER-TECH ACCUSED OF WIDER SPY EFFORT The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant [USN:L6N45Z04V TEXT:"outed Discover-Tech by name"].
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder.
Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software.
Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms .
In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms.
At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech's ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.
TOP ADVERTISER IN YEMEN, SOUTH SUDAN TrendAI's report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running "targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation."
In addition to noting the "obvious skew" towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though "the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero." It said the entity won "an implausibly dominant share" of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela.
TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI's report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said.
Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.
Earlier this year, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, [USN:L6N3Z714C TEXT:"Reuters reported at the time"]. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would cause problems for Palo Alto's operations there, which were already under scrutiny following a Beijing directive ordering domestic companies [USN:L1N3YF0B5 TEXT:"not to use its products"]. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with "procurement regulations in China" and that any suggestion otherwise was "speculative and false."

items.title: Pope Leo to return to his adopted home on South America tour
items.author: Marco Aquino
items.creator: Marco Aquino
items.summary: As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
items.body:
As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
When the pandemic emptied the streets of northern Peru and one of the world's longest quarantines left many struggling to eat, Bishop Robert Prevost, as Leo was known, helped launch a soup kitchen in 2020 in the small town of Zaña.
"He gave us an example of human charity, and we prepared the 'aguadito con fe'," recalled former cook Betty Burga Campos, referring to the traditional soup of rice, meat and vegetables that volunteers served.
Prevost left Peru for Rome three years later after Pope Francis tapped him to lead the Vatican office that recommends candidates for bishop appointments worldwide.
After rising from missionary and bishop in Peru's far north to cardinal and ultimately pope, Leo, 71, is set to revisit the country where he became a citizen and built some of the relationships that [USN:L8N3RH19P TEXT:"defined his ministry,"] weeks after undergoing [USN:L8N45Y19U TEXT:"surgery"] for lung cancer. The Vatican [USN:S8N45H05O TEXT:"confirmed"] on Monday that his November 6 to 17 South America tour remained on schedule.
Across northern Peru, regional governments are refurbishing churches and residents are preparing celebrations for his [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"visit"], which also includes earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
For many Peruvians, memories of the Chicago-born head of the Catholic Church are less about Vatican titles than muddy boots, long drives across the country's rugged north and a hands-on approach to helping people.
"He had become Peruvian, even in the way he spoke. He no longer had much of that American accent," said José Manuel Zamora Romero, a priest in Lambayeque who knew him for years.
The share of adults in Peru who identify as Catholic has fallen from 76% to 67% over the decade to 2024, according to Pew Research Center. The decline is often linked to social changes and distrust of institutions, following years of political instability that have caused Peru to cycle through [USN:S0N3T000N TEXT:"nine presidents"] in a decade.
A BISHOP ON THE MOVE Prevost arrived in Peru in 1985 at age 30. After years based in the United States and Rome with his Augustinian order, he returned in 2014 and became bishop of the Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2015. In 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to the Vatican. Francis named him a cardinal later that year and he was [USN:L1N3RF1DD TEXT:"elected pope"] in 2025.
Across northern Peru's sun-baked farm belt, residents and priests recall a churchman constantly on the move.
For the future pontiff, "the distances were not limits, the distances were opportunities," said David Farfán, a priest in Zaña, one of the towns on the pope's upcoming itinerary.
Many remember Prevost riding horseback to isolated Andean communities. Others recall him driving hundreds of kilometers himself across Peru's rugged north.
"His hobby was driving," Zamora Romero said. "And I know he taught some priests to drive so they could get their licenses ... and they all passed the test."
That practical approach became evident during emergencies.
When severe flooding linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon inundated northern Peru in 2023, photos circulated on social media of Prevost wading through knee-deep water in rubber boots as he helped deliver aid.
When natural disasters occurred, "he was on the front lines to bring the help that the population needed," said Rev. Jorge Villegas of Chiclayo, where the pope will spend two full days.
Residents pointed to moments like those as evidence of a bishop who preferred action over visibility.
"He wasn't very focused on being with the press; he was more with the poor and in social conflicts," said Verónica Castillo, a journalist in Chiclayo who witnessed his intervention during a 2015 labor conflict.
"He was a bishop who intervened, who took action, and people remember that," she added, recalling how Prevost helped mediate the prolonged protest by workers against a sugar company, which turned violent.
'PUT HIMSELF IN SHOES OF A MIGRANT' Migration has reshaped much of Latin America over the past decade, as millions of [USN:S0N3KZ0C4 TEXT:"Venezuelans"] fled economic collapse and political turmoil. Peru hosts the world's second-largest Venezuelan diaspora community, with more than 1.5 million migrants. Many arrived without proper documentation and live with inadequate access to healthcare and basic services.
Prevost founded a Catholic organization in Chiclayo in 2018 to assist newcomers.
"He put himself in the shoes of a migrant first and foremost and knew what the situation was like," said Augusto Martínez, who leads the organization.
The group has assisted thousands of Venezuelans.
As pope, Leo has called for migrants to be treated with dignity, condemned human trafficking and warned traffickers to repent or face divine judgment. He has criticized anti-immigration policies, including measures pursued by US President Donald Trump.
"He supported migrants on how to have a dignified life here in Peru," said Lisbeth Coromoto Díaz, who received help through the Chiclayo organization and said he held Masses in honor of migrants.
Leo's [USN:L6N44L0Y0 TEXT:"planned return"] to Peru has revived hopes among Catholics in Eten, near Chiclayo, that he could advance a long-running campaign to secure Vatican recognition of the town's reported Eucharistic miracle. As bishop, he supported the cause, presenting historical records and thousands of testimonies of faith in Rome, linked to a 1649 apparition in which devotees say the image of the Christ Child appeared in a consecrated host.
Tourism officials are promoting routes tied to the places Leo lived and worked. Souvenir shops are stocking shelves with pope-inspired hats, key chains and pins.
In a shop window in the capital Lima's Gamarra textile district, an image of Leo on a T-shirt depicts him smiling while enjoying a plate of Peruvian food.
"We've got the pope looking spirited; we've got the pope as a foodie, enjoying delicious ceviche and rotisserie chicken. We even have the play on words: 'The Pope and the papa (potato) are Peruvian'," said clothing maker Victoria Quiñones.
Quiñones predicted a 200% increase in her workload and was running low on fabric for the T-shirts.
Nearby, Maria Rodriguez, 70, was shopping for pope T-shirts.
"I’m buying several," Rodriguez said.
"I’ll be wearing them all through November because I am Catholic: Roman and Peruvian," she added.

items.title: La OPEP+ prevé mantener sus metas de producción en la reunión del domingo, según fuentes
items.author: Olesya Astakhova, Ahmad Ghaddar
items.creator: Olesya Astakhova, Ahmad Ghaddar
items.summary: Los países productores de petróleo de la OPEP+ probablemente mantendrán sin cambios sus metas de producción de crudo para diciembre cuando se reúnan el domingo, dijeron a Reuters tres personas al tanto del asunto, mientras el grupo centra su atención en las negociaciones sobre las cuotas para 2027.
items.body:
Los países productores de petróleo de la OPEP+ probablemente mantendrán sin cambios sus metas de producción de crudo para diciembre cuando se reúnan el domingo, dijeron a Reuters tres personas al tanto del asunto, mientras el grupo centra su atención en las negociaciones sobre las cuotas para 2027.
La reunión virtual de siete miembros clave de la OPEP+ —Arabia Saudita, Rusia, Irak, Kuwait, Argelia, Kazajistán y Omán— se celebra mientras los miembros del golfo Pérsico han estado aumentando sus exportaciones, afectadas durante meses por la guerra en Irán, aunque la mayoría sigue produciendo muy por debajo de sus metas.
Las tres fuentes pidieron no ser identificadas y señalaron que aún no se había tomado una decisión definitiva.
La OPEP+ está integrada por la Organización de Países Exportadores de Petróleo y aliados, como Rusia. La OPEP y las autoridades rusas no respondieron de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentarios.

items.title: Crypto blitzes midterms with $176 million to support allies as it prepares for post-Trump era
items.author: Dawn Kopecki
items.creator: Dawn Kopecki
items.summary: The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 midterm races this election cycle, as part of a years-long plan to build a bipartisan coalition of allies in Congress that can advance its interests long after US President Donald Trump leaves office.
items.body:
The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 midterm races this election cycle, as part of a years-long plan to build a bipartisan coalition of allies in Congress that can advance its interests long after US President Donald Trump leaves office.
The $2.75 trillion industry, and the billionaires who built it, are aggressively spending to elect friendly candidates while targeting politicians they see as a threat, according to interviews with more than a half-dozen crypto political strategists and a Reuters review of the spending.
While the industry’s recent spending blitz is known, its long-term plan to further its legislative agenda is less well-understood. The industry isn’t just looking for allies; it is trying to pick candidates who already have a chance of winning, and can help once they get to Congress, the strategists said.
Crypto's largest super political action committee, Fairshake, which spent $196 million during the 2024 election cycle, is leading the industry’s strategy again. Fairshake said 53 of the 58 candidates it supported in primaries or special elections this year won and will be on the ballot on November 3.
Super PACs can accept and spend unlimited sums of money, but cannot coordinate directly with campaigns. They are flooding several races with tens of millions of dollars in ads.
Voters have little way of knowing who pays for these ads, which barely mention crypto. Most of Fairshake's are sponsored by its affiliate PACs with innocuous names like "Defend American Jobs" and "Protect Progress." The ads often focus on hot-button issues like taxes or immigration.
Perceived enemies, such as longtime skeptic Sherrod Brown, vying to return to the Senate in Ohio, can be subjected to an onslaught of often-personal attacks. Advocacy group Public Citizen said crypto was the single-biggest corporate spender in federal races in 2026, after saying in 2024 that its spending was "akin to a corporate Death Star hovering over elections."
The PACs' primary financiers, led by Coinbase, Ripple and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, aren't trying to convince voters to support digital currencies. The money is a calling card to help forge long-term relationships with elected officials, said industry strategists, campaign staff, watchdog groups and political finance managers.
It underscores how the industry is behaving as other businesses do in Washington — using funds to open doors and buffer itself against regulation. The strategy reflects the reality that come 2029, the occupant of the White House is unlikely to be as personally invested in crypto as Trump, whose family made around $2.3 billion from crypto ventures between mid-2024 and April, a Reuters investigation found .
“It's an investment in the future,” said Colin McLaren, head of government relations at crypto industry advocacy group the Solana Policy Institute, which has given $4.9 million to the midterms this year, according to campaign finance records.
The effort is designed to “ensure that over the next 100 years, the crypto industry has clear rules of the road, and that we know what our regulators are expecting from us," he said.
Through October 20, Fairshake and its affiliate PACs have spent about $150.8 million on the midterms this year, while other crypto groups have spent around $25 million, according to campaign finance filings.
"We back pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties, and look forward to continuing to build on the largest pro-crypto caucus in American history," said Geoff Vetter, spokesperson for Fairshake.
COME A LONG WAY In 2018, lawmakers couldn’t even get a room in the House or Senate office buildings to hold the first congressional bipartisan roundtable discussion on crypto, instead meeting across the street from the US Capitol in the Library of Congress, said Kristin Smith, president of the Solana Policy Institute, who helped establish the Blockchain Association that year.
The Biden administration heavily scrutinized the industry following the collapse of FTX and an [USN:L3N2X40RX TEXT:"industry-wide meltdown"] in 2022, with the US Securities and Exchange Commission eventually levying more than $6 billion in penalties in 98 cases, according to a Georgetown University Law study.
“It was an all-out assault on the technology,” said Smith, the Blockchain Association's interim CEO. “The industry was in a corner, and the only way out was to show political force.”
Executives decided they needed a political strategy to combat what they called then-SEC chair Gary Gensler’s “regulation by enforcement,” lobbyists, advocacy groups and campaign strategists said.
Coinbase Chief Policy Officer Faryar Shirzad was the architect behind nonprofit political advocacy group Stand With Crypto — which isn't required to disclose its donors — and Fairshake, which both launched in 2023. The number of Congresspeople with an "A" rating from Stand With Crypto is up to 332, compared with 96 when the group launched.
As the industry has won more legal clarity in Washington, its market value has nearly tripled from around $1 trillion in 2023 to about $2.75 trillion now, according to CoinGecko .
The combination of Trump, a growing bipartisan congressional coalition and a neutered opposition allowed the industry to advance its legislative agenda more in the last two years than some industries have done in decades, other industry lobbyists say.
That includes 2025's Genius Act legislation establishing the first-ever US federal regulatory framework for stablecoins, enacted with overwhelming bipartisan support. That followed a White House meeting earlier in the year when industry leaders, including Coinbase (COIN.O) CEO Brian Armstrong and Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, [USN:L2N3PP0UZ TEXT:"sat with Trump"] when the president declared an end to the "war on crypto."
"Moving that quickly in Washington is like light speed in space," said Ron Bonjean, partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions, and a former senior Senate aide.
The industry's real goal is passing the Clarity Act, which would put crypto oversight under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. That bill stalled in this congressional session and faces an uphill battle next year if Democrats win control of one or more chambers of Congress.
Without it, agency-level [USN:FWN45Q05G TEXT:"regulations undertaken during Trump's term"] can be reversed by a subsequent administration, analysts at JPMorgan said.
Fairshake is financing House candidates from both parties, but it decided to only back Republicans in Senate races after Democrats in that chamber blocked the Clarity Act from advancing to a final vote. Their opposition centered around an ethics provision that would have forced the Trump family to sell their crypto holdings.
Gary Kalman, of anti-corruption nonprofit Transparency International, criticized the bill for shifting regulation to the less-stringent CFTC, and for preempting states from enacting tougher laws.
Coinbase and Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. Ripple didn't return requests for comment.
THE PRIME TARGET Fairshake's highest-profile win in 2024 was defeating Brown, an industry foe who chaired the Senate Banking Committee from 2021 to 2024.
Spending millions attacking the sitting chairman of the industry's oversight committee was unprecedented in Washington, corporate watchdogs and political strategists say. But the gamble paid off.
Now, Brown is running again, with public opinion polls showing him with a narrow lead over his opponent, Republican Jon Husted. The industry has spent more than $68 million on the race, helping to make it one of the most expensive on record, according to AdImpact.
Fairshake’s ads opposing Brown, which it did not comment on, don't mention crypto. One charges him with voting to raise gas taxes in Ohio and raises a [USN:L1N2ZT27M TEXT:"Reuters-debunked claim"] that he voted to "unleash 87,000 IRS agents on you while voting to give social security benefits to illegals."
“Of course, the special interests are panicking, they know Sherrod will fight the rigged system they're feasting on to stand up for working Ohioans,” said Patrick Eisenhauer, Brown's campaign manager.
A CRYPTO MONEY BOMB In some races, crypto spending dwarfed candidate fundraising. The industry spent $5.3 million in a Maryland House Democratic primary to support state Delegate Adrian Boafo, who raised $1.9 million on his own, records show. Other non-crypto groups spent $6.8 million to support Boafo's campaign, which declined to comment.
“There were so many ads ... that it makes other candidates suffocate,” said Quincy Bareebe, a healthcare entrepreneur who came in second of 24 candidates in that primary despite spending $6.6 million of her own money. "Adrian was everywhere."
The industry was less successful in Illinois. Fairshake spent over $10.1 million on ads attacking [USN:L1N4001C8 TEXT:"Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton"], who is running for US Senate, and another $2.5 million against Illinois state Representative La Shawn Ford, who is running for a Chicago-area congressional district. Both are expected to win on November 3.
Ford defeated a dozen primary challengers despite raising just $500,000 and lending his campaign $175,000 to fight off industry-funded ads that brought up a 14-year-old federal indictment that was later dropped. His campaign issued a cease-and-desist letter to Fairshake, accusing it of making defamatory statements about him in its ads.
Fairshake did not comment on its ads or Ford's response. Ford thinks Fairshake targeted him because he supported state legislation to require crypto exchanges and related companies to register with Illinois.
“They were relentless, on every outlet, radio, TV, social media, mailers," Ford said. “It was personal and it was hurtful, and unnecessary for my family to have to go through.”

items.title: フィンランドとノルウェー首脳、ロシア大統領とウクライナ巡り電話会談
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: [ヘルシンキ ２７日 ロイター] -
items.body:
[ヘルシンキ ２７日 ロイター] - フィンランドのストゥブ大統領とノルウェーのストーレ首相は２７日、ロシアのプーチン大統領とウクライナ戦争について電話会談した。フィンランド大統領府が声明で明らかにした。

ストゥブ氏は声明で「率直で実質的な議論だった。われわれはロシアの隣国だ。この戦争の結末は、われわれ両国と欧州全体の安全保障に直接影響する。戦争を終結させるには直接対話が必要だ」と表明した。

ロシアはこれまで、欧州各国がウクライナに武器を供与し、ロシア政府との対話を拒むことで戦争をあおっていると繰り返し非難してきた。

ストーレ氏とストゥブ氏は先週、オスロでウィットコフ米和平交渉担当特使、ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領と会談。ウィットコフ氏はその翌日、ウィトコフ氏はサンクトペテルブルクでプーチン氏と会談した。

ロシア大統領府はプーチン氏とウィトコフ氏の会談後、米国が仲介するウクライナとの和平協議を１１月に再開する意向を表明していた。

items.summary: Wall Street expects Amazon , Microsoft and Alphabet to report on Wednesday faster growth in their cloud businesses, but a turbulent market selloff and concerns over rising costs of AI financing are tempering optimism.
items.body:
Wall Street expects Amazon (AMZN.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Alphabet (GOOGL.O) to report on Wednesday faster growth in their cloud businesses, but a turbulent market selloff and concerns over rising costs of AI financing are tempering optimism.
Investors are pressing for evidence that the AI boom can deliver swift returns to justify its enormous price tag. Rising bond yields at AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave (CRWV.O) and record costs to insure Meta Platform's (META.O) debt have amplified concerns about how the massive AI infrastructure buildout is being funded, particularly as higher US interest rates loom.
Market turmoil has rekindled warnings of an AI bubble from investors, including hedge fund Citadel's founder Ken Griffin, and pushed companies [USN:L6N46216E TEXT:"to delay their IPOs"]. An expected Democratic sweep of the [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"US midterm elections"] could spell more trouble for data centers that are already a target of protests over their impact on power grids, electricity bills and the environment.
Big Tech's results this week will be a litmus test for AI adoption and economic viability. These three companies — with nearly $1.7 trillion in combined backlog — plan to spend as much as $600 billion this year.
Meta's results last week showed just how unforgiving the calculus has become. Better-than-expected revenue growth and an upbeat outlook were overshadowed by increased spending plans, sending its shares down nearly 7% the following day. They are now down more than 4% this year.
"The appetite for capital expenditure alone is slowing rapidly," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management.
"For Amazon, Google and Microsoft specifically the growth in their cloud companies is a very important line item that will signal if further growth in capital expenditure can be funded without further risks of contracting free cash flow."
While the trio's stocks have outperformed ad-driven Meta this year, with gains ranging from 1.2% to 10.1%, they continue to lag behind the S&P 500's near 12% rise.
Google Cloud is expected to again lead the three major players in the September quarter, with revenue surging 95.1% to $29.57 billion, according to LSEG data. That would be faster than the 81.8% growth in the previous quarter.
Amazon Web Services, the market leader in cloud, is expected to post 38.2% revenue growth, up from 36.8% in the previous quarter. Microsoft Azure is expected to expand 47.7%, accelerating from 42% three months earlier, according to Visible Alpha data.
Alphabet and Amazon are expected to burn cash for the second and third consecutive quarters, respectively, while Microsoft will likely generate more than $8 billion in cash flow.
GOOGLE CLOUD SUCCESS, SEARCH CONCERNS Alphabet's cloud business and in-house chips have emerged as a bright spot in its AI push amid concerns Google's models are falling behind those of OpenAI and Anthropic. But competition from personal AI agents such as Meta's Muse as well as chatbots such as ChatGPT has raised concerns about the search business that has long powered its earnings.
Google search revenue growth is expected to slow to 14.7% from 16.8% in the previous quarter, even as total revenue is expected to rise at a slightly faster pace of 25.2% to $128.18 billion.
"This quarter, we believe commentary is equally important to quantitative results as competition for search is growing again with agents while there is increased consternation around the payback of AI capital expenditure," Citizens analyst Andrew Boone said.
MICROSOFT CHANGES REPORTING SEGMENTS Microsoft will report under a revamped structure for the first time on Wednesday, combining cloud, AI and business software into a division called "Agents and Infra", and Windows, gaming and ad sales into another dubbed "Devices and Consumer".
A notable change will be the disclosure of Azure's quarterly revenue, resolving investor frustration over its previous focus on growth rates without absolute figures.
Analysts expect Azure to post sales of $33.06 billion in the quarter, powering a 16.7% rise in Microsoft's total revenue to $90.66 billion, slightly slower growth than the previous period.
Amazon's overall revenue growth is expected to slow to 12.3% from 19.6% in the previous quarter.

items.title: India seeks bigger share of diesel exports on refining capacity boom
items.author: Nidhi Verma
items.creator: Nidhi Verma
items.summary: India's diesel exports are set to surge from 2027, giving the South Asian nation a bigger role in global markets, as state-run companies boost refining capacity, industry officials said on Tuesday.
items.body:
India's diesel exports are set to surge from 2027, giving the South Asian nation a bigger role in global markets, as state-run companies boost refining capacity, industry officials said on Tuesday.
That will bolster India's position as a [USN:L4N44A0C1 TEXT:"swing supplier"] of refined products in an already tight global market buffeted by the US-Iran and Ukraine-Russia wars that have disrupted trade flows and boosted freight rates worldwide.
"We will be in a happy situation of not only refining for ourselves but for the world," said Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri.
India is becoming a global refining hub as it prepares to boost refining capacity to 300 million tons per year by 2030, and increasing further to 400 million tpy later.
Amid unprecedented disruption to global refining from conflict and plant closures, with operating refineries running at historic utilisation rates to ease fuel shortages, India has emerged as the second-largest exporter of seaborne diesel this year, behind only the US, ship-tracking data from Kpler shows.
In 2027, Indian state refiners will together increase their diesel production capacity by 16.5 million tons as they boost capacity of existing refineries, officials said.
"We will be exporting diesel due to refinery expansion," said A S Sahney, chairman of Indian Oil Corp, the country's largest refiner, which aims to add about 18 million tons of annual capacity, to produce about 8 million tpy of additional diesel.
Hindustan Petroleum Corp's new 9-million-tpy refinery in the western state of Rajasthan will turn out 3 million tpy of diesel next year, once the refinery stabilises, said Chairman Vikas Kaushal.
Bharat Petroleum Corp plans to produce 1.5 million tpy extra diesel from next year, its chairman, Sanjay Khanna, said.
Oil India's subsidiary Numaligarh refinery in the eastern region, which will be expanded to 9 million tpy in March next year, will add 3 million tpy of diesel production.
Some refiners, such as HPCL, buy refined products from private companies for sale by their retail outlets. The expansion will limit their purchases from other companies for local sales, and free up volumes for exports, officials said.
Additionally, India's expanding refining capacity is designed to process a broad range of crude grades and flexible petrochemical feedstocks, letting companies capitalise on price arbitrage and produce higher-value products.
Private refiners Reliance and Nayara now export refined fuels while state companies mainly meet domestic demand.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described India as a refining "superpower" during a recent visit to Reliance's massive refining complex in the port city of Jamnagar.
Puri said India aimed to become a global refining hub with fuel demand expected to rise to drive its economic expansion.
